thread.title: Dow, S&P 500 suffer worst one-day fall in five months as Apple drags

title: Dow, S&P 500 suffer worst one-day fall in five months as Apple drags
text:
Dow, S&P 500 suffer worst one-day fall in five months as Apple drags Tuesday, 2018-01-30 02:44:52 Font Size: | Print Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US on January 26, 2018. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Font Size: | 
Wall Street pulled back from record highs on January 29, with the Dow and the S&P 500 indexes marking their biggest one-day percentage declines in about five months, weighed down by a slide in Apple shares. 
Shares of Apple (AAPL.O) fell 2.1 percent on news that the company will halve production of its US$999 iPhone X smartphone. The company is due to report earnings on February 1. 
The S&P technology index .SPLRCT fell 0.9 percent and was the biggest drag on the benchmark index following Wall Street’s strongest four-week run since 2016. 
The Cboe Volatility Index .VIX, the most widely followed barometer of expected near-term volatility for US stocks, closed up 2.76 points, or nearly 25 percent, at 13.84, its highest close since August 18. 
Benchmark US 10-year Treasury note US10YT=RR yields hit their highest since 2014 due to economic strength, which added to pressure on defensive sectors such as utilities, real estate and telecoms. 
The Dow Jones Industrial Average .DJI fell 177.23 points, or 0.67 percent, to 26,439.48, the S&P 500 .SPX lost 19.34 points, or 0.67 percent, to 2,853.53 and the Nasdaq Composite .IXIC dropped 39.27 points, or 0.52 percent, to 7,466.51. 
The Dow and S&P 500 had their biggest daily percentage declines since September 5. The S&P 500 still is up 6.7 percent since the end of 2017. 
It was a rocky start to an action-packed week, which will feature US President Donald Trump’s first official State of the Union speech late January 30. 
Also ahead this week is the Federal Reserve’s meeting, the US employment report and earnings from a host of high-profile names including Amazon.com (AMZN.O), Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Facebook (FB.O). Reuters
